JSON: Name: dat_tri_structural_pipeline Title: Cryo-EM–guided structural and functional mapping of triple-reuptake inhibitor binding modes to the human dopamine transporter to determine residue-level determinants of inhibition and conformational stabilization Short Hypothesis: Binding of a triple-reuptake inhibitor to specific central-pocket residues (for example D79, F326, S422) causally stabilizes DAT in either an outward- or inward-facing conformation, and that conformational stabilization directly determines inhibitor potency (IC50) for DAT. Related Work: Prior approaches include single-ligand structural determinations of monoamine transporters and pharmacological profiling of TRIs and classic inhibitors. Existing structural studies resolved transporter conformations with select inhibitors and substrates, and separate pharmacology work measured inhibitory potency across DAT/NET/SERT. Limitations in current methods are: lack of systematic, multi-ligand, multi-conformation structural ensembles for DAT across diverse TRI chemotypes; scarce matched functional validation (mutagenesis + uptake kinetics) for structure-derived interactions; limited direct structural comparisons across MATs with identical ligands to explain selectivity; insufficient dynamic/energetic analysis linking static binding poses to conformational stabilization or kinetic on/off rates; and inadequate ablation studies addressing specific chemical moieties' roles. These gaps hinder rational optimization of TRI scaffolds toward desired potency and transporter selectivity. Abstract: Understanding how chemically diverse triple-reuptake inhibitors (TRIs) bind monoamine transporters and stabilize distinct transporter conformations is critical for rational antidepressant design. We propose an integrated structural–functional pipeline that combines high-resolution cryo-electron microscopy of human DAT bound to multiple TRI chemotypes, matched [3H] dopamine uptake assays with systematic pocket-directed mutagenesis, and molecular dynamics simulations in lipid bilayers. The pipeline will generate an ensemble of ligand-bound DAT structures spanning outward- and inward-facing states, quantify the effect of specific residue substitutions on inhibitor IC50 and kinetics, and compute dynamic stability and energetics of ligand–transporter complexes. The main contribution is a residue-level blueprint linking TRI chemical features to conformational stabilization and inhibitory potency, enabling prediction of potency and selectivity changes from structural modifications. Expected outcomes include a validated set of structural determinants (e.g., D79, F326, S422) predictive of TRI behavior and a dataset for structure-guided optimization of next-generation MAT-targeted antidepressants. Experiments: Datasets: (1) Cryo-EM raw movies and processed maps for human DAT complexes with tesofensine, dasotraline, centanafadine, ansofaxine, and nefazodone (target: ≥2.8–3.5 Å reconstructions), DAT apo, and comparison datasets: NET+tesofensine and SERT+tesofensine maps; (2) Functional datasets: [3H] dopamine uptake dose–response curves for WT and mutant DAT constructs (biological n≥3); (3) MD trajectory datasets: three independent 100-ns production replicates per selected complex (nefazodone, tesofensine, dasotraline) in a POPC:cholesterol membrane. Baselines: (A) Known DAT inhibitors (cocaine, GBR12909) structural and functional profiles; (B) DAT apo and non-binding control mutants (e.g., distal-surface mutants). Mutant panel (minimum): D79A, F76A, F326A, S422A, V152A, L329A, E428A, G323A, G426A. Evaluation metrics: cryo-EM global resolution, local map-to-model FSC, ligand pose RMSD, per-residue B-factor/occupancy; uptake assay IC50 and Hill coefficient, fold-change vs WT; kinetic assays where possible: kon/koff (radioligand association/dissociation or SPR); MD metrics: ligand RMSD, MM/PBSA binding energy estimates, TM1a tilt angle, intracellular cavity opening distance. Experimental setup: expression of N-terminal truncated and full-length human DAT in HEK293F with identical constructs used for EM and uptake; purification, nanodisc reconstitution (brain polar lipids + cholesterol or defined POPC:cholesterol), ligand incubation (concentrations: 10 μM for cryo-EM unless ligand-limited; higher where used in report), grid freezing and collection on 300 kV Krios with K3 detector, image processing in cryoSPARC, map refinement and model building in PHENIX/Coot. Functional uptake: transiently transfected HEK293F, uptake buffer as specified in report, [3H] dopamine range for IC50 determinations 10 pM–100 μM, technical triplicates and biological triplicates; statistical tests: two-sided unpaired t-tests for mutant vs WT IC50 fold-changes and ANOVA for multi-group comparisons. Comparisons/ablations: (i) group comparison of outward-facing–stabilizing ligands (tesofensine, dasotraline) vs inward-facing ligands (centanafadine, ansofaxine, nefazodone) on TM1a tilt and IC50 distributions; (ii) mutational ablation of aromatic pocket (F326A, F76A) to test role in dichlorophenyl/tropane anchoring and measure fold-change in IC50; (iii) chemical ablation: test ligand analogs lacking dichlorophenyl or ethoxymethyl moieties to measure pose shifts and functional effect; (iv) cross-MAT test: tesofensine in DAT vs NET vs SERT structures and IC50 measurements. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical failure modes: poor cryo-EM particle orientation distributions or extreme conformational heterogeneity preventing high-resolution reconstruction; incomplete ligand occupancy or ligand dissociation during grid preparation yielding ambiguous density; mutations destabilizing global fold rather than specifically perturbing ligand interaction. Data and evaluation biases: use of HEK293F expression and nanodisc composition may not replicate neuronal lipid environment or post-translational modifications, affecting transporter conformation and ligand interactions; truncation of N-terminus may bias intracellular gating conformations. Scalability and compute limits: cryo-EM data collection and processing demand high instrumentation time and compute; MD simulations limited by timescale and unable to sample slow conformational transitions deterministically. Limitations to generalization: residue-level determinants identified for DAT may not fully extrapolate to NET and SERT despite conservation; in vitro inhibition potency and conformational stabilization may not predict in vivo pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, or clinical tolerability. Methodological assumptions: MM/PBSA energy estimates and force-field parameters for ligands may produce quantitative errors; measured IC50 changes may reflect indirect effects (e.g., expression level) if not strictly controlled.
